questions.q: What comparison does the author use for not exercising?
a: It is like taking a depressant
It is like skipping breakfast
It is like aging too quickly
It is like catching a cold
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the author compares a sedentary life to taking a depressant, since movement lifts mood and reduces stress.

questions.q: What does the author think doctors should try before prescribing medication?
a: Encouraging the patient to exercise
Sending the patient to a nutritionist
Recommending a longer period of rest
Suggesting a change of workplace
questions.why: Lesson 1 says doctors should first push patients toward sport and movement rather than man-made drugs.

questions.q: Which diet does the summary recommend relying on common sense to choose?
a: Mostly vegetables, plant proteins and plant fats
Mostly lean meat, fish and dairy products
Mostly whole grains with moderate sugars
Mostly fruit with occasional processed snacks
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes a diet built around vegetables and plant-based proteins and fats, with less tobacco, alcohol and caffeine.

questions.q: Which country does the summary cite as an example of a long-living nation?
a: Japan
Italy
Mexico
Sweden
questions.why: Lesson 2 names Japan among cultures with healthy diets and plenty of exercise that live notably long lives.

questions.q: What does the summary say about genes and a long, healthy life?
a: Genes matter, but nutrition and habits also shape lifespan
Genes alone decide how long a person will live
Genes have almost no influence on life expectancy
Genes can be completely rewritten through exercise
questions.why: Lesson 3 argues that genes play a major role, yet whole populations with better diets and habits live longer.
